2. The plaintiffs filed a suit being Title Suit No. 327 of 1961 in the 1st Court of Munsif at Perojpur for establishment of their title to 4 annas share in the suit land and for confirmation of their possession therein. They also made an alternative prayer for recovery of possession of that land, if they were found to be out of possession. Their case was that the land of C.S. Plot No. 929 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 149 of mouza Kalakhali under P.S. Perojpur, District Barisal belonged to Ekramullah to the extent of 8 annas, Islam Sikdar and Kalim Sikdar to the extent of 4 annas each in Karasha right. The 4 annas share of Islam Sikdar devolved upon the plaintiffs and that of Kalim Sikdar was inherited by his daughters defendant Nos. 18 and 19. Ekramullah granted a Patta in 1305 B.S. in Kol Karsha right in respect of his 8 annas share to Alimuddin and Tasiluddin, predecessors-in-interest of defendant Nos.1 to 12. In Augrahayan, 1368 B.S. corresponding to December, 1961 the defendants threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession whereupon the aforesaid suit was filed. 

 “It is not disputed that property in C.S. Khatian No. 149 is still ejmali. Hence all the co-sharers have shares and possession in all the land of the Khatian. The C.S. Khatian No. 149 shows that the dag No.929 was recorded in the sole possession of Ekram. There is no specific case of ouster or adverse possession by Ekram in the dag. There is no convincing evidence on record in this respect. Hence, all the co-sharers have their shares in this dag as well as in all the plots of C.S. Khatian No. 149.” 

 6. Mr. Pal urged that although it was found that Ekramullah alone possessed C.S. plot No. 929 and now the lessees under him have been possessing the same, the first appellate Court as well as the High Court erred in holding that the said possession amounted to adverse possession to the knowledge of the appellants and that it constituted ouster. He argued that it is neither unusual nor inconceivable that a co-sharer may keep in his sole possession certain plot of a joint holding. This possession simply amounted to sole possession of a co-sharer and such sole possession does not amount to exclusive or adverse possession constituting ouster. He pointed out that Khatian No. 149 contains several plots including the suit pot No. 929 and it is not disputed that the land of this Khatian is still joint among the co-sharers. He further pointed out that joint possession of all the co-sharers was recorded in Khatian No. 149 according to their shares vide Ext. D. But the kolkarsha of the respondents in plot No. 929 was recorded under Ekramullah. Nevertheless the legal title that is Karsha right of the other co-sharers in respect of this plot was not affected. The respondents cannot claim more than Kolkarsha right which they took settlement of from Ekramullah. They did not ever deny the superior karsha right of Ekramullah. The appellants claim their karsha right along with their co-sharer Ekramullah. In this view of the matter it was urged that the Courts of appeal below erred in dismissing the suit on the finding that the title of co-sharers had been lost due to adverse possession of the respondents. In support of his contention he relied upon some decisions. In Bindu Bala De Vs. Rebati Mohan De (4 DLR Dac. 239) the question arose about the effect of a record standing in the name of one of the co-sharers of a joint property. It was contended that the properly was in exclusive possession of the person in whose favor the record stood. It was, however, held "if a joint property is recorded in the possession of one of the co-sharers, the effect of the record is that it was in the sole possession of that co-sharers and it would not raise an inference that it was in his exclusive possession or in his possession adversely to the other co-sharers as sole possession is not exclusive or adverse possession" It is in conformity with the well settled principle of law that possession of one co-sharer is in point of law the possession of all co-sharers. In Arjun Chandra Vs. Jogendra Chandra (13 DLR Dac. 565) there was a question as to whether the transferee from a co-tenant was on the same footing as original tenant in the matter of the rules governing relations between tenants in common. It was observed that transferee from a co-tenant was on the same footing as the original tenant in the matter of the rules governing relations between tenants-in-common. The rule that possession of a co-sharer is presumed to be non-adverse against the other co-sharers is applied to the transferees as well. The possession by a co-owner of a joint property is perfectly lawful as he is not only entitled to his undivided share but to the whole of the property. There is, therefore, no bar for an owner of an undivided share to the property to be in possession of the whole of that property, but his possession on basis of legal right cannot be adverse to the other co-sharers. The learned counsel thus submitted that the same principle must govern the case of lessees from a co-sharer of a joint property so far as their possession is concerned. Reliance was placed on a decision reported in  A.I.R. 1936 P.C. 183 (Pannambala Vs. Periyanan) with a view to show that possession of lessees does not become adverse till something is done repudiating tenancy. He, therefore, rightly urged that the possession of the respondents in the suit land being under a co-sharer of the appellants, however long and continuous this possession may be, it cannot be adverse so long hostile title is not set up by the lessees against their own lessor and that is possible only after repudiation of the tenancy. It may be noted that the respondents did not ever deny the title of their lessor Ekramullah.
